title: The abandoned elder house office is not dramatic rescue. It is bathing, food, medication, listening, dementia repetition, death preparation, and the daily refusal to make age a reason for discard.
The addiction threshold office refuses to make dignity wait for sobriety. It asks what love looks like before recovery is stable and while overdose remains near.

The border-waiting office is the kitchen, warehouse, woodpile, charged phone, rights observer, and night response that stay with people while the official door remains closed. It must never turn people in exile into volunteer scenery.
The child-of-the-imprisoned office protects the child from becoming a public extension of a parent’s conviction. The cleanest form of this office reduces labels and preserves ordinary belonging.

The chosen-family-for-trans-and-queer-adults office is the cube's second chosen-family office and the first focused on adults already pushed out of biological family. The threshold is the moment the trans woman, gay man, or queer migrant arrives without housing — released from prison, evicted with a hotel closure, fleeing a homicidal country — and discovers that someone has built her a house. The danger of the office is that "chosen family" can be aestheticised into spectacle; the office must remain a place where the person can leave, refuse the script, and not be photographed for it.

The civil-identity-threshold office is the inverse of name-after-death: it is name-before-life. Without registration, a child cannot enter the first school, the first clinic, the first job, the first bank, the first border. The threshold is paperwork the state has chosen not to issue; the office is the slow, repetitive, decades-long labour of producing a self the state will recognise.

The collapsed-state-neighborhood-kitchen office is mutual. The helper is also being helped. The threshold is the moment public utilities, hospitals, ambulances, and international aid all withdraw or are denied access — and the neighbourhood decides to keep cooking. This is not vertical mercy; it is horizontal survival, and the cube must not flatten it into "heroism" because the volunteers are themselves at risk of being killed for serving food.

The disconnected-dead-no-kin office answers a problem the migrant-grave office does not: a person who lived in a wealthy society long enough to age, run out of relatives, and outlive the fee structure that would have kept their grave. The threshold is the absence of a successor. The office is interment together — bones combined into a statue, ashes interred under shared trees — so that "alone" stops being the last word on the life.
The distress-call witness office receives coordinates, fear, water, silence, and institutional delay. It is witness under time pressure, not glory.

The doctrinal-return-after-captivity office is not individual but communal. A religious authority decides that the survivor of forced conversion and sexual enslavement remains a member of the community, and writes that decision into doctrine. The threshold is the temple gate; the office is the rebaptism, the public welcome, the refusal to let the perpetrator's verdict become the community's. The danger is that the welcome arrives partial, with limits the community has not yet been willing to face — and the cube must hold both the welcome and its limits in the same hand.
FAMILY-LED JUSTICE AFTER TRC DELAY
GBV HEALTH FIRST RESPONDER AND EVIDENCE CHAIN
GBV SAFENET REFERRAL MESH
The HIV house office receives the person whose body has been turned by family and culture into a feared sign. The office counters stigma by table, room, medicine, and chosen kin.
HOMESHARE NIGHT-PRESENCE

The humanitarian corridor office is safe legal passage where the death route has become normalised: identification, visa, flight, housing, language, school, medical care, and integration. Its danger is the list: who is selected, who waits, and who remains outside.
ISLAND COUNSELLOR STANDARDS AND CAPACITY GAP

The island crisis-line office is the phone, text, face-to-face listening, and community psychological-first-aid layer before a person is alone with suicidal distress. It is small enough to answer, but must be checked for reach, referral capacity, language, and volunteer support.
LAW TO DOOR — FAMILY PROTECTION IMPLEMENTATION

The migrant grave office refuses the double border: first the border that risked death, then the burial system that requires money, kin, and paperwork. It asks whether the stranger dead will be treated as someone or as disposal logistics.
The name-after-death office says the failure to save a life must not become the failure to remember the life. It is necessary, but it is not enough.
NORTH PACIFIC FIRST CRISIS COUNSELLING CENTRE

The overdose-memorial office is parallel to but distinct from the name-after-death office for the unhoused. The double stigma of illicit substance and "their own fault" prevents many families from grieving openly. The threshold is the funeral or vigil at which the family discovers whether the death will be permitted into the public record without footnotes. The office is silver ribbon, candle, named reading — and the refusal to let "overdose" be a moral verdict on the life.
PACIFIC FEMINIST CRISIS CENTRE AND REFUGE
PACIFIC ISLAND CRISIS-LINE AND POST-DISASTER MHPSS

The pain-relief-at-dying office faces a state that has decided morphine is more dangerous than untreated death. The threshold is a prescription pad and a doctor who is willing to risk professional consequence to use it. The office must accept that politics will sometimes ask it to choose between proximity to power and purity of position — and that the dying patient cannot postpone their pain while the office answers that question.
The parent-reorientation office keeps the child from having to carry the parent through the parent’s fear. The adult finds peers, language, and courage elsewhere so the child can remain the child.

The Pasifika suicide-prevention/postvention office is family, fono, church, youth, language, and community champion before it is programme vocabulary. It must be culturally specific without pretending Pasifika is one culture.

The peer-led-psychiatric-crisis office is held by people who have themselves heard voices, been hospitalised, been medicated, been refused, and decided to make a place for the next person. The threshold is the moment a voice-hearer realises they are not alone and not necessarily ill — that "hearing voices" is a meaningful human experience some 2-4% of the population shares without psychiatric contact. The office is not anti-psychiatry; it is anti-monopoly. The danger is that the office is read as a complete substitute for clinical care when crisis demands both; the cube records that the office adds to, rather than subtracts from, the toolkit available to the person in crisis.

The private sponsorship settlement circle is a group of ordinary people signing themselves into rent, groceries, forms, appointments, and a year of availability. Its danger is dependency: the door can become patronage unless the sponsored person can refuse the script.
PROTECTED ELDER HOUSING / ANTI-INSTITUTIONAL ORDINARY DWELLING

The psychological-distress-call office is the cube's domestic sibling of the migrant distress-call witness. Both are phones that stay on. But where the migrant distress call is short and concerns coordinates, this call is long and concerns whether the person on the line will be alive tomorrow. The office must be both available and bearable — the volunteer or counsellor at the other end is part of the threshold. In compounding-crisis contexts (collapsed currency, explosion, war, displacement, pandemic) the office may be the last functioning service the state has not absorbed; this is also its danger.
REGIONAL TRAINING AND STANDARDS BACKBONE

The religious-exit-ramp office is the rare departure from a violent organisation that the organisation itself will permit. In the Salvadoran and Honduran case, gangs do not let members retire; the exits are emigration and conversion. The office is a church door that stays open under accusation of being "a pastor for gangsters," and a pastor who keeps opening it though the state of emergency is arresting his congregation. The danger is that conversion becomes a precondition for dignity, and that the surveilled visible-piety the gang demands replaces one set of bars with another; the cube must hold the office and the precondition together without letting one cancel the other.

The return-of-the-disappeared-dead office gives a hidden body back to kin, name, ceremony, and place. It can restore dignity without settling justice; reburial must not be made to stand in for prosecution, reparations, or truth.
The safe-exit door office must be especially careful. A person exiting exploitation may need options, safety, harm reduction, income, law, housing, and time—not a rescuer’s preferred narrative.

The search-for-the-disappeared office takes up the work the state has refused. It does not wait for an investigator; it brings a shovel, a phone, a vigil. The threshold is the moment "missing" stops becoming "actively searched for" — and the office holds that threshold open with the labour of relatives who are themselves at risk of being made to disappear.
SERVICE GAP MAP AND NEGATIVE SPACE

The suicide-postvention office serves not the dying but the bereaved. Exposure to a suicide raises the risk of further suicides; the office is therefore prevention by another name. The threshold is the survivor's first day after the death, and the office sits with the family for years rather than weeks. Where the office is indigenous-led, it may also be recovering a pre-colonial framework in which suicide was met with compassion rather than shame — the office reframes the stigma the survivor did not invent.
SURVIVOR CASE-MANAGEMENT AND SAFE-HOUSE DOORWAY

The unclaimed-child-burial-and-naming office answers the threshold after a child dies without a claimant able to carry burial, name, and public memory; its danger is that posthumous dignity can become posthumous ownership.

The unfinished-TRC office refuses to let a public ritual of truth become a private sentence of non-recognition. It stays after the commission, after the cameras, after the state says the case is closed.

The public-cemetery-record-and-family-access office turns state burial from anonymous disposal into searchable record, visit, and story; its danger is that searchable memory can become surveillance, art capture, privacy harm, or false return.

The street-medicine house-call-to-the-unsheltered office moves the clinic threshold to the person outside; its danger is that outreach can become surveillance, medicalized poverty management, or a substitute for housing.
